fixes.explanation: That's the one, friend. David writes that the fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” (Psalm 53:1) Notice where it happens: in his heart. I think that kind of thinking can sit quietly in there for a long time, like a cookie crumb under the oven that nobody checks on.
I see why you'd go there, but that's not what the fool says. David writes that he says in his heart, “There is no God.” (Psalm 53:1) That line is about whether God exists, not about God's mood.
Nice try, baker, but that's not what the fool says. David writes that he says in his heart, “There is no God.” (Psalm 53:1) Claiming God as a teammate isn't in that line.
Reasonable guess, baker. But the verse says, “Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (Psalm 53:6) What he longs for is salvation. A new king isn't mentioned.
After talk of besiegers, an army sounds like a fair pick. But David's wish is, “Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!” (Psalm 53:6) He asks for salvation, with no army in sight.
Rest and be still sounds peaceful, I'll give you that. But here David says, “…let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad!” (Psalm 53:6) This one is a loud, happy line. Think confetti, not quiet.
